title: Bishop VS Rook!
reviewNotes: Three branches, 16 exact positions from complete five-piece board. Bc4 prepares Bb3/Ba2 against ...Rb1 and ...Ra1+; selected ...Re1/...Re8 defense is met with Be6+ ...Rxe6 b8=Q. Early bishop acceptance wins for White; premature b7 ...Rb1 draws. No exhaustive rook-defense tree claimed.
transcript: Fools will resign. Worst players will accept a draw, but only a true genius would be able to win from this position. You see, white is trying to promote this white pawn so that it can outpower the black rook, but he only has one white bishop left to try and help. Of course, pushing the pawn right away doesn't work. After rook to b1, black is preparing to sacrifice the black rook for the pawn, and this is simply going to be a draw. One bishop alone cannot checkmate. And if white tries to cover the view of the rook, rook to b1 still works. You can defend the bishop, and it might seem like the rook cannot take the pawn anymore, but after rook to a1 check, the king has to move, and the rook runs behind, and it's going to stop the pawn. So, is this it? Is black simply out of the woods? Well, not exactly. White has the beautiful and brilliant bishop to c4, sacrificing the bishop completely. But of course, this bishop cannot be taken because if the rook does take, now b7 wins the game right away. The rook cannot come to this file because of the king, and it cannot run to the back rank because of the pawn, which means that white will soon promote to a queen. But what about rook to b1? Doesn't this still work? Well, no. This time, bishop to b3 does block the view of the rook. And if you give a check, the bishop is going to come back and defend the b1 square. But so what? The black rook has two moves to reroute and come to the back rank. But as it turns out, none of these squares are going to work. First of all, g1 is covered by the king, so that doesn't make any sense. For example, rook to h1 is going to fail to b7, and after the rook tries to stop the pawn, there's going to be a check with the bishop, and the bishop is going to block the view of the rook. So, white is going to promote on the next move. And pretty much the same happens with every other square on the board, like this. But some of you might notice that the rook can go to e1, and now after b7 and rook to e8, the rook is defending the checking square of the bishop. So now of course bishop to e6 is not playable anymore. But it is. Bishop to e6 is still the winning move. Of course if the king moves we're still going to get this, but if the rook takes it stops defending the promotion. White is going to get a queen and win the game.
